p3c1.essay:
For two parts the book has hardly left Raskolnikov's side, and I had stopped noticing how airless that was until this chapter opened a window. He issues his ultimatum, turns to the wall, and the novel does something new: it walks out of the room and down the stairs with other people. What we get on the landing is close to farce. Razumihin, drunk and newly lovestruck, crushes the ladies' hands 'as in a vise', kneels on the pavement, and half-strangles the doctor for calling Dounia 'fetching'. I find it a real relief, and I think Dostoevsky means it as one. This is what a loud, decent, unguarded person looks like, and after so many chapters inside a concealment it is like hearing a different instrument.

The comedy is carrying freight, though. Before he collapses Raskolnikov says of the marriage, 'Let me act like a scoundrel, but you mustn't... one is enough.' His family hears a sick man's harshness. We hear a confession in code. He has understood since [[p1c4|his first reading of his mother's letter]] that Dounia is selling herself for his sake, and now he forbids it in the tone of a man who knows from inside what a ruined life is. Razumihin roars 'Despot!', and that is fair too.

Then there is the speech on the pavement, which is funny and which I take entirely seriously. 'To go wrong in one's own way is better than to go right in someone else's.' Razumihin is raging at friends who 'live on other people's ideas', and he has no notion that the friend he has just put to bed is the most extreme case in the city of a man possessed by an idea. Whether that idea is Raskolnikov's own nonsense or someone else's is a question the book keeps pressing. Here it is asked by accident, by a drunk man, of two women who only want to know whether their Rodya is all right.

Notice also that Dostoevsky stops to describe Dounia and her mother at length, which he rarely bothers to do for anyone. Dounia is her brother over again: the pacing, the pride, the same face made beautiful. The mother has 'a certain barrier' she will not cross. Lines, barriers and who steps over them: the family vocabulary is the book's vocabulary.

The chapter ends on Razumihin's hymn to the landlady's parlour, 'as snug as though you were dead, and yet you're alive'. It is a joke about feather beds. It is also a description of a comfortable way of not living, delivered a few yards from a room where someone is trying a much less comfortable one.

annotations.quote: It revealed an emotion agonisingly poignant, and at the same time something immovable, almost insane.
annotations.note: Two things at once in one face, which is how the mother will go on seeing him for the next three chapters: the son she recognises and something fixed behind him that she does not. 'Immovable' is the word I would underline. Whatever he feels for them, it is not going to change what he has decided.

annotations.quote: Let me act like a scoundrel, but you mustn’t... one is enough...
annotations.note: To his mother this is fever talking. To us it is very nearly a statement of fact: the family already has one member who has done something unforgivable for the family's sake. He is forbidding Dounia to follow him, without being able to say where he has gone.

annotations.quote: it was characteristic of Razumihin that he showed his true nature at once, whatever mood he might be in
annotations.note: A plain sentence, and a pointed one in this book. Razumihin is legible in ten minutes; his best friend has become unreadable to his own mother. Dostoevsky sets the two side by side all through Part Three, and the contrast does a good deal of quiet work.

annotations.quote: To go wrong in one’s own way is better than to go right in someone else’s.
annotations.note: The best line of a drunk man's lecture, and I think the novel half agrees with it. 'I am a man because I err' is his cheerful version of the old Latin tag about erring being human. What gives it an edge is that he is saying it about parlour radicals, an hour after tucking in a friend whose error is of another order entirely.

annotations.quote: In face she resembled her brother, but she might be described as really beautiful.
annotations.note: The resemblance is more than a family detail. Dounia has his pride, his habit of pacing while she thinks, and that slightly haughty lower lip; watch how often, from here on, the two of them behave like one temperament arguing with itself.

annotations.quote: there was a certain barrier fixed by honesty, principle and the deepest convictions which nothing would induce her to cross.
annotations.note: The narrator steps forward to say this about Pulcheria Alexandrovna, who can seem merely fluttery. She will yield and yield, and then stop. In a novel about a man who decided a barrier was there to be crossed, a mother defined by the one she will not cross is not an accident.

annotations.quote: anxieties, apprehensions, troubles, certain ideas... and so on.
annotations.note: Zossimov is showing off for Dounia, and yet buried in his list is the right diagnosis. 'Certain ideas' is exactly what is wrong with the patient. The doctor says it and sails straight past it, pleased with his own bedside manner.

annotations.quote: “That’s a fetching little girl, Avdotya Romanovna,” remarked Zossimov, almost licking his lips
annotations.note: Garnett's 'fetching' has gone a little quaint, but the leer comes through. After ten minutes of grave professional reserve upstairs, this is what the reserve was covering, and Razumihin's hands are round his throat before the sentence is cold.

annotations.quote: as snug as though you were dead, and yet you’re alive--the advantages of both at once!
annotations.note: The climax of a wonderful catalogue: pancakes, fish-pies, the samovar, warm shawls, and the 'three fishes' on which folk belief said the world rests. Razumihin means it as a sales pitch for a quiet life with the landlady. Set it beside the cramped room upstairs and its tenant, and 'dead, and yet alive' sounds less cosy.

links.why: Raskolnikov's ultimatum here is the spoken version of what he raged to himself on first reading the letter: that he will not accept Dounia's sacrifice.
The scene Razumihin keeps describing to the ladies, Luzhin's visit and dismissal, as it actually went.
The argument Razumihin stormed out of at his party, about living on other people's ideas, gets taken up again there sober and at length.

p3c2.essay:
A morning-after chapter, and Dostoevsky is very good on the specific shame of it. Razumihin wakes knowing two things: that something 'unlike anything he had known before' has happened to him, and that he behaved like a lout while it was happening. His solution is to wash scrupulously and then refuse to shave, in case anyone should think he had shaved on purpose. I love this. It is self-consciousness so elaborate that it comes out as a kind of innocence, and it is the comic mirror of his friend upstairs, who also calculates what every gesture will make people think, for much darker reasons.

Two documents sit at the centre of the chapter, and they are worth reading against each other. The first is Razumihin's spoken portrait of Raskolnikov: 'morose, gloomy, proud and haughty', kind-hearted, and yet at times 'simply cold and inhumanly callous; it's as though he were alternating between two characters.' It is the most accurate thing anyone has said about him, and it comes from the person who knows least about what he has done. (The surname helps here if you have a little Russian: raskol is a split, a schism.) The second is Luzhin's letter, which damns itself without assistance. Count the times he has 'the honour', then look at what the honour is wrapped around: an order to a mother to keep her son out of the room, a threat, and a piece of spying dressed up as concern for her purse. In [[p1c3|Pulcheria Alexandrovna's own letter]] we saw Luzhin through her hopeful paraphrase. Now we have his prose, and it is worse than [[p2c5|his conversation]].

What interests me most is Zossimov's little lecture. He has a theory, and it is a good one: a poor, vain, feverish student is insulted at the police office by a suspicion, and broods on it until it becomes a monomania. Every fact fits. It is the wrong answer reached by sound method, and it does Raskolnikov the enormous service of explaining away exactly the behaviour that ought to be noticed. Keep an eye, too, on the two words 'And Porfiry.' Zossimov thinks Zametov talked too much last night, and he remembers who was listening.

The mother gets the last notes: her dream of Marfa Petrovna in white, her fear of her own son, and then the landlady's door open a crack, with 'two keen black eyes' behind it. Nearly everyone in this novel is being watched by someone.

annotations.quote: He brought his fist down heavily on the kitchen stove, hurt his hand and sent one of the bricks flying.
annotations.note: Razumihin's remorse is physical, like everything else about him; he punishes a stove. Keep the bruised hand in mind, because Dostoevsky pays the joke off before the chapter is over.

annotations.quote: What if they think that I shaved on purpose to...? They certainly would think so! Not on any account!
annotations.note: He cannot even finish the sentence to himself. The logic is perfect and absurd: he must look clean out of respect, but not so clean as to suggest hope. I find this one of the most exact pictures of being newly in love that I know.

annotations.quote: These monomaniacs will make a mountain out of a mole-hill... and see their fancies as solid realities....
annotations.note: The young doctor has assembled a tidy case history: rags, fever, an insulting suspicion at the police office, and a proud man brooding on it. We know the mole-hill is not a mole-hill. A plausible medical story is forming around Raskolnikov, and it shelters him better than any alibi he could invent.

annotations.quote: he shouldn’t have told all that last night. He is an awful chatterbox!
annotations.note: The next two lines are the ones to hold on to: 'But whom did he tell it to? You and me?' 'And Porfiry.' Razumihin shrugs it off. Zossimov, who is no fool when he is not preening, does not sound as if he does.

annotations.quote: it’s as though he were alternating between two characters.
annotations.note: Razumihin has known him a year and a half and has seen what we have seen since the first chapter: the man who empties his pockets for strangers and the man who is 'inhumanly callous'. He offers it as a puzzle, not a diagnosis, and I think the book wants us to keep it as a puzzle too.

annotations.quote: “He loves no one and perhaps he never will,” Razumihin declared decisively.
annotations.note: Said by the one person who has nursed him for nothing, and said to his sister, so it lands hard. I do not think Razumihin is right, but I notice the novel lets the charge stand unanswered. Dounia changes the subject by asking what he means, and he changes it again by blurting that she is just like her brother.

annotations.quote: God forgive me, I simply rejoiced at her death.
annotations.note: A shocking thing for this gentle woman to say, and she knows it. The dead fiancee, sickly and plain, first surfaced in his statement at [[p2c1|the police office]]. What the mother remembers is that nothing, not her tears or their poverty, would have stopped him once he had decided.

annotations.quote: he gave twenty-five roubles on the pretext of the funeral, which gravely surprised me knowing what pains you were at to raise that sum.
annotations.note: The poison in the letter. Luzhin was evidently there to see [[p2c7|the scene at the Marmeladovs']], and he reports it to the mother bent into the ugliest shape it will take: her sacrifice, handed to a girl 'of notorious behaviour'. Note that he knows to the rouble what the family scraped together, and thinks it his business.

annotations.quote: must have looked then every inch a queen and even more a queen than at sumptuous banquets and levées.
annotations.note: Presumably Marie Antoinette in her last prison. It is a student's bookish comparison, and a sweet one, prompted by holes in a pair of gloves. He was terrified of Dounia because she was poor, not in spite of it; her poverty is what makes her unanswerable.

annotations.quote: two keen black eyes were watching them from the darkness within.
annotations.note: Our only real glimpse of Praskovya Pavlovna, the bashful landlady who has hovered offstage since the first page: a pair of eyes and a slammed door. After last night's talk about her jealousy it is a good comic exit, and also one more instance of somebody looking on from the dark.

links.why: The mother's long letter gave us Luzhin in her words; put it next to the letter he writes himself here.
What actually happened with the twenty roubles and the 'young woman of notorious behaviour', before Luzhin retold it.
The police-office scene Zossimov builds his whole theory on, and the place where the landlady's daughter was first mentioned.

p3c3.essay:
I think this is one of the most painful chapters in the book, and almost nothing happens in it. A young man who has been ill receives his mother and sister, whom he has not seen for three years. He is washed, combed and polite. He apologises, he kisses them, he holds out his hand to his sister at exactly the right moment. And Dostoevsky tells us through the doctor's eyes what all this is: 'a sort of bitter, hidden determination to bear another hour or two of inevitable torture.'

The chapter's method is to let us watch one performance from five chairs. Zossimov sees a case improving. Razumihin sees a 'sentimental mood' and loves him for it. The mother sees generous impulses and fine eyes and then, in the middle of her own delight, 'I'm afraid! Why, what am I afraid of?' Dounia sees most: 'Is he being reconciled and asking forgiveness as though he were performing a rite or repeating a lesson?' And Raskolnikov, inside the performance, makes the bleakest observation of all: 'Yet in their absence I seemed to love them so much.' That sentence seems to me truer and sadder than anything he says aloud. He could love them as figures in a letter, people to be rescued. Sitting three feet away and wanting to be talked to, they are unbearable, because they are owed the one thing he cannot give.

What that thing is, the chapter states outright at its centre. He tells his mother, 'We shall have time to speak freely of everything!' and the words turn to ice as he says them: he sees that 'he would never again be able to _speak_ of anything to anyone.' Garnett keeps the italics, and they matter. It is the feeling that first came over him in [[p2c1|the police office]] and again [[p2c2|on the bridge]], and it is the real form his punishment has taken so far. Nobody has caught him. What has happened instead is that ordinary speech has turned into lying. He gets up and walks to the door without a word, which is the honest response, then sits down and shouts at everyone to talk, which is the only one available.

Notice how much of the conversation brushes the wound without anyone intending it. He mentions, idly, that he forgot to have Nastasya 'wash out the blood'. His mother says his room is 'like a tomb'. Zossimov prattles about actions performed cunningly while their direction is deranged. And Dounia, defending her marriage, cries 'I am not committing a murder,' and her brother goes white. She means it as the most far-fetched comparison she can find. The irony is not subtle and Dostoevsky does not want it to be: we are the only ones in the room who can hear.

Then comes the exchange I would single out, because it is where his private theory leaks into family talk. He confesses giving away the money and adds that to help others 'one must have the right to do it'; the French tag he tosses after it means, roughly, die like dogs if you are not satisfied. When Dounia refuses to agree, he mutters about reaching 'a line you won't overstep'. Hold on to that verb. The Russian word for crime in the title means, at its root, a stepping-over, and Garnett's 'overstep' keeps the root in view. He is speaking to his sister about her choices and to himself about something else, and his verdict on both sides of the line is the same: unhappy if you stop, 'still unhappier' if you cross. From a man who crossed on principle, that is a remarkable thing to let slip.

The quarrel over Luzhin is where brother and sister turn out to be one temperament. Both are proud, both flush, each accuses the other of lying, and Dounia lands the blow he cannot answer: 'Why do you demand of me a heroism that perhaps you have not either?' And then, abruptly, he loses interest. 'Marry whom you like!' I do not read that as generosity. It is the thousand miles opening up again; he looks at his own passionate concern for her and cannot remember what it was for.

What brings him back is, of all things, a prose style. Handed Luzhin's letter, he turns critic: the legal jargon, the threat folded inside the courtesy, the slander with its 'too obvious display of the aim'. It is the steadiest his mind has been in a long while, and it is steady because the subject is another man's bad faith. 'To act sensibly, intelligence is not enough,' he says of Luzhin. I doubt he hears himself.

annotations.quote: a sort of bitter, hidden determination to bear another hour or two of inevitable torture.
annotations.note: This is a reunion with a mother and sister after three years, and the word chosen for it is torture. Dostoevsky routes the observation through Zossimov, who sees the fact clearly and has no idea of the reason. That split, right symptoms and wrong cause, governs the whole scene.

annotations.quote: I forgot yesterday to ask her... Nastasya... to wash out the blood... I’ve only just dressed.
annotations.note: He says it as a domestic excuse for being late, and the room stops. It is Marmeladov's blood, innocently come by in [[p2c7]], and he can explain it perfectly. But listen to how the word arrives, in that halting rhythm, in front of his mother. He cannot keep it out of his mouth.

annotations.quote: “Perhaps it’s a good thing really that he should think me almost a madman,” thought Raskolnikov.
annotations.note: A cold little calculation in the middle of a family visit. The doctor's theory of deranged purpose and cunning execution is on offer as cover, and he takes note of it. A few lines earlier he was answering 'with special carefulness'. He is never just talking.

annotations.quote: if you reach a line you won’t overstep, you will be unhappy... and if you overstep it, maybe you will be still unhappier....
annotations.note: The most important sentence in the chapter, thrown away in irritation. 'Overstep' is the book's key verb; the Russian word for crime is built on it. He offers Dounia a choice between two unhappinesses and then is 'vexed at being carried away', as well he might be. He has just told her how his own experiment feels from the far side.

annotations.quote: that he would never again be able to _speak_ of anything to anyone.
annotations.note: The punishment in the title, as it stands at this point: not prison, not even fear, but being shut out of plain talk with the people he loves. The lie that triggers it is the kindest thing he says all morning, a promise to his mother that they will have time to speak freely.

annotations.quote: I seem to be looking at you from a thousand miles away
annotations.note: He begins by saying the dead girl is 'in another world' and ends by putting his living mother and sister there too. The drift from one to the other is unplanned, and it frightens him enough that he cuts himself off with 'what's the use of asking about it?'

annotations.quote: If only you knew, though, what a strange thing you said just now, mother
annotations.note: She has called his room 'like a tomb' and blamed it for his melancholy. He does not say what is strange, and I would not press it too hard, but the garret has been the place where his idea was hatched since [[p1c3]], and he has just described himself as a man looking at the living from somewhere else. He laughs 'strangely', which in this novel is rarely a good sign.

annotations.quote: If I ruin anyone, it is only myself.... I am not committing a murder.
annotations.note: Dounia reaches for the most extreme thing she can think of that she is not doing, and hits her brother exactly. It also happens to be the best argument against him: her sacrifice, whatever one thinks of it, spends only herself. His near-faint recalls [[p2c1|the one at the police office]], and his mother's 'You have made him faint' gets a sharp, frightened denial.

annotations.quote: What am I making such a fuss for? What is it all about? Marry whom you like!
annotations.note: A minute ago it was 'me or Luzhin'. Now he looks at Dounia 'with a sort of wonder', as if someone else had been doing the shouting. It is Razumihin's 'two characters' caught in the act of changing over, and it is more unnerving than the anger was.

annotations.quote: He is a man of intelligence, but to act sensibly, intelligence is not enough.
annotations.note: His verdict on Luzhin, delivered at the end of a genuinely shrewd reading of the letter. It is also, word for word, a verdict on a clever student who reasoned his way to an axe. I cannot tell whether Dostoevsky wants us to think he notices; I rather think he does not.

links.why: The police office, where he first felt he could no longer speak openly to another human being, and where he fainted as he almost does here.
The moment on the bridge when he felt he had cut himself off from everyone, which this family visit proves true.
The mother's letter, where Marfa Petrovna, Svidrigaïlov and Luzhin were first introduced, and where these two women were still easy for him to love.
The scene is interrupted rather than concluded; read straight on.
